concepts.name: Constitutional Basis of Parliamentary Sessions: Article 85 and Its Limits
key_dimensions: Article 85 empowers the President to summon, prorogue, and dissolve — but does NOT mandate specific number or names of sessions
The '6-month gap' rule between two sessions and its constitutional origin vs. conventional practice
Distinction between summoning (President's role) vs. actual scheduling (Cabinet's recommendation)
UPSC trap: Constitution does not use the terms 'Budget Session', 'Monsoon Session', or 'Winter Session' — these are purely conventional

concepts.name: Summoning, Prorogation, and Dissolution: Distinctions and Consequences
key_dimensions: Summoning: begins a session; Prorogation: ends a session but not the House; Dissolution: ends Lok Sabha's existence
Effect on pending bills and business — bills lapse on dissolution but NOT on prorogation (key UPSC trap)
Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved — implications for business continuity across sessions
President acts on Cabinet's aid and advice under Article 74 — no independent discretion in summoning

concepts.name: Budget Session: Constitutional Imperatives and Structural Design
key_dimensions: Article 112 mandates presentation of Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget) — not 'Budget Session' per se
Two-part structure: Part 1 (Feb 1 – recess) and Part 2 (post-recess to May) and the rationale for the recess
Presentation of Railway Budget (merged with Union Budget since 2017) and its significance
Vote on Account vs. Full Budget: Article 116 — Vote on Account allows interim spending before full Budget passage

concepts.name: Union Budget Presentation: Date, Timing, and Recent Reforms
key_dimensions: Shift from last working day of February to February 1 (since 2017) — reasons and implications for spending cycle
Advance presentation allows ministries to operationalize schemes from April 1 (start of financial year)
Budget presented first in Lok Sabha (Article 109/110) — Rajya Sabha has no voting power on Money Bills
UPSC trap: Budget is not a Money Bill per se — it is a combination; Appropriation Bill and Finance Bill are separate

concepts.name: Vote on Account, Interim Budget, and Full Budget: Overlaps and Distinctions
key_dimensions: Vote on Account (Article 116): grants advance authorization from Consolidated Fund for a few months — no policy changes
Interim Budget: presented in election year; covers full financial year; can include policy announcements (though conventionally avoided)
UPSC trap: Vote on Account ≠ Interim Budget — Interim Budget includes full revenue and expenditure estimates; Vote on Account is only expenditure authorization
No constitutional bar on policy announcements in an Interim Budget — purely a convention (Model Code-related)

concepts.name: Monsoon Session: Conventional Timing, Business, and Accountability Functions
key_dimensions: Typically July–August; no constitutional mandate for this specific session
Historically used for legislative business deferred from Budget Session and passage of supplementary demands
High density of Question Hour, Zero Hour, and Opposition-initiated debates — accountability mechanism
UPSC angle: Adjournment Motions and Calling Attention Motions are more frequent in Monsoon Session — procedural distinctions

concepts.name: Winter Session: Business, Declining Frequency, and Constitutional Concerns
key_dimensions: Typically November–December; constitutionally optional but conventionally regular until recent years
Cancellation of Winter Session 2020 and 2023 — raised concerns about the 6-month gap rule and democratic accountability
Winter Session historically used for passage of pending bills and ratification of ordinances (Article 123 requirement)
UPSC trap: If Winter Session is not held, ordinances promulgated in September must be ratified in the next session (Budget Session) within 6 weeks

concepts.name: Ordinance-Session Nexus: Article 123 and Session Timing
key_dimensions: Ordinance ceases to operate 6 weeks after reassembly of Parliament — session timing directly affects ordinance validity
President can promulgate ordinance only when both Houses are NOT in session (or one House is in session for joint matters)
Re-promulgation of ordinances without Parliamentary approval: DC Wadhwa case (1987) — unconstitutional fraud on Constitution
UPSC trap: Ordinance lapses if Parliament is in session but does NOT pass it — or if disapproved by resolution

concepts.name: Recess vs. Adjournment vs. Prorogation: Procedural Hierarchy
key_dimensions: Adjournment: suspends sitting for hours/days — business can resume; moved by Presiding Officer
Recess: break within a session (e.g., Budget Session recess) — session continues technically
Prorogation: terminates the session by Presidential notification — pending notices/motions (except bills) lapse
UPSC trap: Adjournment sine die (indefinite adjournment by Presiding Officer) ≠ Prorogation — President must separately prorogue

concepts.name: Lapsing of Bills Across Sessions: Rules and Critical Exceptions
key_dimensions: Bills pending in Lok Sabha lapse on dissolution; bills passed by Lok Sabha but pending in Rajya Sabha also lapse on dissolution
Bills pending in Rajya Sabha do NOT lapse on dissolution of Lok Sabha (Rajya Sabha is a continuing House)
Bills do NOT lapse on prorogation — they carry over to next session of the same Lok Sabha
UPSC trap: President can notify that certain bills passed by one House need not lapse under Article 108 (Joint Sitting provision)

concepts.name: Question Hour and Zero Hour: Procedural Rules and Session Context
key_dimensions: Question Hour: First hour of every sitting; Starred (oral), Unstarred (written), Short Notice Questions — constitutional backing via Rules of Procedure
Zero Hour: Immediately after Question Hour; no mention in Rules of Procedure or Constitution — purely conventional (since 1962)
UPSC trap: Zero Hour has no constitutional or statutory basis — cannot be 'suspended' through a formal rule — yet routinely practiced
Private Member's Business: Fridays in both Houses — distinction between Private Member Bills and Government Bills in session scheduling

concepts.name: Supplementary Demands for Grants and Excess Grants: Session-linked Financial Control
key_dimensions: Supplementary Demands (Article 115): presented when Budget allocation proves insufficient — usually in Monsoon/Winter Session
Excess Grants (Article 115(1)(b)): for expenditure already incurred exceeding sanctioned amounts — requires PAC report first
Token Demands and Vote of Credit — special provisions under Article 116 for exceptional circumstances
UPSC trap: Supplementary Demands require full Parliamentary approval like the original Budget — not just Cabinet authority

concepts.name: Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, and Session Approval Requirements
key_dimensions: Consolidated Fund (Article 266): all revenues and borrowings — withdrawal requires Parliamentary appropriation through Appropriation Bill
Contingency Fund (Article 267): imprest account operated by President — advances for urgent unforeseen expenditure WITHOUT prior Parliament approval
Contingency Fund expenditure must be recouped through Supplementary Demands in the next session
UPSC trap: Contingency Fund is NOT outside Parliamentary control — only the initial advance bypasses it; subsequent ratification is mandatory

concepts.name: Joint Sitting (Article 108): Trigger Conditions and Session Implications
key_dimensions: Triggered when: Rajya Sabha rejects a bill, passes with amendments Lok Sabha disagrees with, or delays beyond 6 months
Joint Sitting called by President via notification; Speaker of Lok Sabha presides
UPSC trap: Joint Sitting is NOT available for Money Bills (Article 110), Constitutional Amendment Bills (Article 368), or Financial Bills involving appropriation
Only three Joint Sittings in history: Dowry Prohibition (1961), Banking Service Commission (1978), POTA (2002) — factual anchor

concepts.name: Parliamentary Privileges and Their Application During Sessions
key_dimensions: Freedom of speech in Parliament (Article 105): absolute immunity for anything said or vote cast — no court jurisdiction
Privilege applies only during the session and within Parliament's precincts — lapses outside
Breach of privilege and contempt of House: House can punish — but courts have intervened (Searchlight case, Raja Ram Pal case)
UPSC trap: Article 105(3) privileges are those of British House of Commons as of 1950 UNTIL Parliament codifies them — never fully codified

concepts.name: Guillotine: Time-Allocation and Passage of Demands Without Discussion
key_dimensions: Guillotine: all outstanding Demands for Grants are voted upon en masse on the last day of discussion without debate
Business Advisory Committee allocates time for discussion of Demands — if time runs out, Speaker applies Guillotine
UPSC angle: Guillotine undermines financial scrutiny — a structural weakness of Parliament's budgetary control
Cut Motions (Policy Cut, Economy Cut, Token Cut) can be moved against Demands — but rarely succeed as Treasury Benches dominate

concepts.name: Finance Bill vs. Appropriation Bill: Passage Rules and Constitutional Differences
key_dimensions: Appropriation Bill (Article 114): authorizes withdrawal from Consolidated Fund — cannot be amended to increase any amount or alter its destination
Finance Bill: gives effect to taxation proposals in the Budget — classified as Money Bill under Article 110
UPSC trap: Not all Finance Bills are Money Bills — Finance Bills with provisions beyond Article 110(1) are 'Financial Bills (Category II)' and can be introduced in Rajya Sabha
Appropriation Bill must be passed before financial year ends; if delayed, Vote on Account bridges the gap

concepts.name: Role of Presiding Officers in Session Management: Speaker and Chairman's Powers
key_dimensions: Speaker adjourns Lok Sabha sine die; Chairman adjourns Rajya Sabha sine die — distinct from Presidential prorogation
Speaker's power to disallow questions, regulate business, certify Money Bills (Article 110(3)) — final and non-justiciable
UPSC trap: Speaker's certification of a bill as Money Bill cannot be challenged in courts (Article 110(3)) — confirmed in Nabam Rebia case
Pro-tem Speaker: appointed by President to administer oath to new members before regular Speaker is elected — powers are limited

concepts.name: Parliamentary Committees and Session Cycle: DRSCs, PAC, and Estimates Committee
key_dimensions: Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs): 24 committees that examine demands for grants BEFORE they are presented to Parliament — budget scrutiny role
Public Accounts Committee (PAC): examines accounts AFTER expenditure — reports tabled in session; no time limit on its work
Estimates Committee: examines whether policy implicit in estimates is sound — works across sessions continuously
UPSC trap: DRSCs examine budget demands but their recommendations are NOT binding on the government — only persuasive

concepts.name: Special Sessions and Extended Sessions: Constitutional and Practical Dimensions
key_dimensions: No 'special session' category in Constitution — any session called outside convention (e.g., Special Session for GST midnight launch 2017) is still a regular session under Article 85
Extension of sessions: Business Advisory Committee recommends; President issues fresh notification — no limit on session length
Night sittings and extended hours during session: used frequently during Budget Session for passage of Finance/Appropriation Bills
UPSC angle: Declining number of sitting days (from ~120 days in 1950s to ~60-70 days recently) — accountability deficit concern
